approved: Communications Legislation Amendment (Deregulation and Other Measures) Bill 2019
Written by a model from the explanatory memorandum; not the record
The bill would cut red tape in broadcasting and telecommunications while keeping consumer protections.
It would change reporting rules, classification standards, and numbering management, and let the minister pick an industry body to run numbering instead of the ACMA.
The bill would also let NBN companies sell surplus non-communications goods to anyone and remove NBN Co's power to issue fibre installation statements.
Remove duplicate reporting requirements for licensees and controllers to the ACMA.
Let the minister appoint an industry-based numbering manager instead of the ACMA.
Stop the ACCC from issuing tariff filing directions to carriers and service providers.
Allow NBN companies to sell surplus non-communications goods to any person.
Repeal NBN Co's ability to issue statements about not installing fibre in new developments.
Abolish the ACMA's requirement to consult an advisory committee before declaring submarine cable protection zones.
Broadcasters, telecommunications carriers, service providers, NBN companies, the ACMA, the ACCC, and the minister.

The bill reduces regulatory burdens on broadcasting and telecommunications, corrects a payment error for Network Investments Pty Ltd (increasing transitional support from $632,000 to $819,000 per year plus an additional $187,000 annually for five years), and allows the minister to appoint an industry body to manage telephone numbering instead of the Australian Communications and Media Authority.

Labor will not oppose the Communications Legislation Amendment (Deregulation and Other Measures) Bill 2019, but moved a second reading amendment criticising the government for presenting a "do-nothing" bill originally drafted in 2015 and failing to deliver outcomes from a spectrum reform process started over four years ago.

The speaker seconded the Communications Legislation Amendment (Deregulation and Other Measures) Bill 2019, arguing it is a minor deregulation exercise that does little to address major media challenges such as declining local news, 106 newspaper closures from 2008-2018, and a $3.7 billion advertising revenue shift to digital platforms. The speaker called attention to the government's inaction on regional media decline, NBN failures, $366 million in ABC funding cuts, and warned that weakened local journalism threatens democratic engagement.

The speaker supported the deregulation bill as a minor housekeeping measure but argued it fails to address major communications challenges, criticising the government for cutting $366 million from the ABC and lacking a plan for the digital economy and independent media viability.

The Communications Legislation Amendment (Deregulation and Other Measures) Bill 2019 reduces regulatory burden on broadcasting and telecommunications industries, including increased transitional support payments for network investments, a single classification scheme for free-to-air TV, removal of duplicative notification requirements, and repeal of over 50 spent acts, while maintaining consumer and competition safeguards.
